title: Dependency Caching
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of dependency caching and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to dependency caching.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on dependency caching. Dependency caches save rebuildable inputs using keys and restore prefixes; a cache miss should affect performance, not correctness. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Dependency Caching matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Artifacts preserve files produced by a run; caches accelerate reconstruction of dependencies. They serve different purposes and neither should contain secrets.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Dependency caches save rebuildable inputs using keys and restore prefixes; a cache miss should affect performance, not correctness. Artifacts preserve files produced by a run; caches accelerate reconstruction of dependencies. They serve different purposes and neither should contain secrets. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Why caching is useful
items.text: For why caching is useful, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Cache keys
items.text: Cache rebuildable dependencies using a key that includes the package manager, runtime/OS as appropriate, and lockfile hash. A cache miss must not change build correctness, and secrets do not belong in caches.

items.title: Restore keys
items.text: Use a scoped token, validate request inputs and event payloads, check HTTP/error status, handle pagination and rate limits, and avoid logging credentials or unneeded private response data.

content_blocks.code:
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
    with:
      node-version: "20"
      cache: npm
  - run: npm ci
  - run: npm test
content_blocks.expected_output: The setup action configures Node and dependency caching based on the npm lockfile; the tests still run even when there is a cache miss.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use this only in a Node project with a committed lockfile and test script. Review action source/pinning policy for production use.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain dependency caching, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Choose between short-lived outputs, persisted artifacts, and reusable dependency caches.

The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
